message.content:
Research the DATA / PRIVACY model that WhatsApp bot platforms declare in their terms and privacy policies. Use WebSearch and WebFetch extensively. Target these platforms' own legal/privacy/DPA pages: Wati, Landbot, Manychat, Respond.io, Chatfuel, Twilio, 360dialog.

Find concrete, sourced answers to:
1. Who is the "data controller" vs "data processor" in these platforms' terms? Typically the business customer is controller, the platform is processor. Confirm with each platform's DPA / terms language and quote it.
2. How do they describe who "sees" or can access the message content? Do they acknowledge the platform/operator technically has access to message content?
3. Encryption: do they claim encryption at rest / in transit? Note that Cloud API messages are decrypted at the business/BSP endpoint (end-to-end encryption of consumer WhatsApp does NOT extend to the business's server side once received). Find Meta/BSP statements on this.
4. Access controls: what do they say about employee access, sub-processors, data retention.
5. How do they phrase to their own CUSTOMERS that the platform can access messages (transparency language)?

Return a bullet list of falsifiable claims, each with a source URL. Quote exact language from DPAs/privacy policies. Note uncertainty.

<message to="telegram-mg-17804">
Research briefing: data/privacy model in Wati and Landbot legal docs. Every claim below is sourced to a page I fetched; where a page couldn't be pulled or wording was ambiguous, I flag it.

## WATI (Clare.Ai Limited, trading as Wati.io)

**1. Controller vs processor**
- "'Controller' means the entity which... determines the purposes and means of the processing of personal data." / "'Processor' means an entity which processes personal data on behalf of the controller." — business customer = Controller, Wati = Processor.
Source: https://www.wati.io/dpa/
- "If there is a conflict between the provisions of the Agreement and this DPA, the provisions of this DPA shall prevail." (Sec. 2)
Source: https://www.wati.io/dpa/

**2. Who can access message content**
- "Clare.Ai Limited designs its systems to only allow authorized persons to access data they are authorized to access based on principles of 'least privileged' and 'need to know'." (Annex II)
Source: https://www.wati.io/dpa/
- Role-based access to chats is acknowledged: "Role-based access control allows businesses to limit which team members can see chats." (search-surfaced from Wati security material; not verified verbatim on a fetched Wati page — treat as PLAUSIBLE, not confirmed.)
- Honest gap: neither the GDPR help article nor the security-overview page I fetched contains an explicit sentence saying "Wati/the operator can technically read message content." They speak of least-privilege access, not a disclosure that staff can see content.

**3. Encryption**
- In transit: "Clare.Ai Limited makes HTTPS encryption (also referred to as SSL or TLS) available for data in transit." (Annex II)
Source: https://www.wati.io/dpa/
- At rest: NOT explicitly specified with a standard. DPA only requires "appropriate technical and organizational measures for protection of the security, confidentiality, and integrity of the Personal Data." (Uncertain — no at-rest encryption clause found.)
Source: https://www.wati.io/dpa/

**4. Access controls / sub-processors / retention**
- Personnel: "required to execute a confidentiality agreement in writing at the time of hire and to protect Customer Personal Data at all times." (Annex II)
- Data isolation: "Each Wati customer's data is stored in a separate database." / "Each Wati instance runs in its own Docker container with a dedicated network." / "Audit log files are read-only and require the appropriate permissions to access or view them." / "Backups are stored in Google Cloud Platform (GCP) Storage Buckets across multiple regions."
Source: https://support.wati.io/en/articles/11463219-wati-security-overview-data-protection-backups-and-hosting
- Sub-processors (Annex III): WhatsApp, Meta for Business, Instagram for Business, Google Cloud Platform, MongoDB, Cloudflare, ElasticSearch, OpenAI, Google (Gemini), Deepgram, Intercom.
Source: https://www.wati.io/dpa/
- Retention: UNCERTAIN — two fetches of the same DPA gave different wording ("within ninety (90) days... return... or... deleted" vs "delete... as soon as reasonably practicable following the end of the Agreement"). Verify the exact clause on the live page before quoting.
Source: https://www.wati.io/dpa/ (last updated Apr 30, 2025)

## LANDBOT (HELLO UMI, S.L.)

**1. Controller vs processor**
- "The purpose of this clause is to regulate the relationship between the Client, in its capacity as Data Controller, and Landbot, in its capacity as Data Processor." (Terms, Sec. 10.1)
Source: https://landbot.io/terms-conditions
- Processor duty: "Process personal data only in accordance with documented instructions from the Client, including with respect to transfers of personal data." (Sec. 10.7a)
Source: https://landbot.io/terms-conditions

**2. Who can access data / message content**
- Strong customer-facing claim: "Users are the exclusive owner of the data at all times, so only the Users and their Teammates can access the data."
Source: https://help.landbot.io/article/h2ndzk6som-privacy-security
- "Landbot will never share your data with third parties, unless it's necessary for the performance of our Services." (same page)
- Note: this "only Users and Teammates can access" framing is a business-facing assurance; the help page "does not contain specific information about... employee access controls" and directs to security@landbot.io. So the claim that the operator itself has no technical access is asserted but not technically substantiated on the page (flag as customer-assurance language, not a technical guarantee).

**3. Encryption**
- Privacy policy: "Pseudonymise and encrypt personal data, where appropriate." (Sec. 8.3.o.4) — conditional ("where appropriate"), not an absolute at-rest/in-transit guarantee.
Source: https://landbot.io/privacy-policy
- Terms, archived data: "The system maintains data stored securely in an encrypted secondary database preserving metadata and key conversation attributes." (Sec. 10.5.3)
Source: https://landbot.io/terms-conditions
- The security help page "does not contain specific information about encryption at rest, encryption in transit." (Uncertain / not stated there.)
Source: https://help.landbot.io/article/h2ndzk6som-privacy-security

**4. Access controls / hosting / sub-processors / retention**
- Confidentiality: "persons authorised to process personal data undertake, expressly and in writing, to respect confidentiality." (Privacy 8.3.g) and "Maintain the duty of secrecy... even after the provision of the Services has ended." (8.3.f)
Source: https://landbot.io/privacy-policy
- Hosting: "All instances are located in Google's servers in Belgium, Europe (Google Cloud Engine, west-1)."
Source: https://help.landbot.io/article/h2ndzk6som-privacy-security
- AI tools access acknowledged: "non-sensitive personal data... may be processed by these tools when our employees use them for legitimate business purposes." (Privacy Sec. 6)
Source: https://landbot.io/privacy-policy
- Sub-processors: "The Controller authorises the Processor to carry out the following subcontracting necessary to provide the Services," with change notice "at least 20 calendar days in advance." (Privacy 8.3.e)
Source: https://landbot.io/privacy-policy
- Retention: "Personal data... will be archived and permanently deleted 3 years from the date of account deactivation"; "Financial data... 6 years." (Privacy 8.3.q). Help page adds: "Once data is deleted from your Landbot account, it will be permanently erased from our servers, and no restoration will be possible."
Sources: https://landbot.io/privacy-policy and https://help.landbot.io/article/h2ndzk6som-privacy-security

## Key contrast for your briefing
- Both use the standard controller/processor split (customer = controller, platform = processor), verbatim-confirmed for both.
- Landbot markets a stronger "only you and your teammates can access the data / exclusive owner" line to customers — but that's an assurance, and its own privacy policy elsewhere admits employees/AI tools may process personal data "for legitimate business purposes." That tension is the most falsifiable, quotable point.
- Neither platform, in the pages I could fetch, plainly tells its customers "our operators can technically read your message content." Both lean on least-privilege / confidentiality language instead. That silence is itself a finding.
- Encryption: Wati confirms in-transit (HTTPS/TLS) but no explicit at-rest standard. Landbot only says "encrypt... where appropriate" plus an encrypted archive DB — weaker/conditional. Neither states a clear at-rest encryption guarantee in what I fetched.

Flagged uncertainties: Wati retention exact wording (two conflicting fetches); Wati "team members can see chats" quote (search-surfaced, not verified on a live Wati page); the DPA at trust.landbot.io / Vanta is gated (couldn't fetch the full standalone DPA — I used the Terms Sec. 10 and privacy policy which carry the processor clauses).
</message>

# DATA / PRIVACY MODEL — Respond.io & Twilio (sourced, verbatim)

## Important sourcing caveat up front
- **Respond.io's actual DPA is NOT public.** respond.io/dpa returns 404; the real page (respond.io/data-processing-agreement) only says the DPA is available on request via privacy@respond.io. So the controller/processor clause could not be verified from a fetched Respond.io document. The controller/processor definitions I quote below come from Respond.io's **Privacy Policy**, not a signed DPA. Flagged explicitly per item.
- Twilio's DPA, Security Overview, WhatsApp docs, and the Meta Cloud API doc WERE fetched and quoted directly.
- Twilio DPA quotes carry section labels as returned by the fetch model; I did not independently re-verify each section number against the raw page, so treat section numbers (not the quoted text) as lower-confidence.

---

## RESPOND.IO

**1. Controller vs. processor** — *(from Privacy Policy, NOT a DPA; the DPA is gated behind email request, so the customer=controller / respond.io=processor allocation could NOT be verified from a public Respond.io doc)*
- Definitions only: Controller = "The natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body which, alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes and means of the processing of Personal Data"; Processor = "The natural or legal person... which processes personal data on behalf of the Controller."
  Source: https://respond.io/privacy-policy
- UNVERIFIED: no fetched Respond.io page explicitly states "Customer is Controller, Respond.io is Processor." That allocation would live in the on-request DPA.

**2. Who can access message content**
- Privacy Policy: "Some data may be accessible to certain internal staff (such as administration, sales, marketing, legal, and IT) and to external parties."
  Source: https://respond.io/privacy-policy
- Security page: "Under no circumstances is sensitive data shared with anyone outside of respond.io and the client." (Note the phrasing — it acknowledges respond.io itself, alongside the client, is inside the access boundary.)
  Source: https://respond.io/security
- No fetched page contains an explicit sentence like "Respond.io staff can read your message content." The access is implied by the staff-access and "outside of respond.io and the client" language, not stated bluntly.

**3. Encryption**
- Security page: "respond.io uses 256-bit SSL/TLS encryption. At rest, respond.io content is protected using 256-bit AES encryption."
  Source: https://respond.io/security
- Privacy Policy (in transit only): "We use TLS encryption to secure data transfers on our website." (No at-rest claim in the Privacy Policy itself; the at-rest claim is on the Security page.)
  Source: https://respond.io/privacy-policy

**4. Access controls / sub-processors / retention**
- Employee access (Privacy Policy): internal staff with access = "administration, sales, marketing, legal, and IT."
  Source: https://respond.io/privacy-policy
- Sub-processors (Privacy Policy): "Processors bound by our data protection instructions include service providers... They have been carefully selected and authorised, and are monitored regularly"; list "available upon request."
  Source: https://respond.io/privacy-policy
- Hosting (Security page): "Respond.io is a cloud-based solution, Amazon Web Services (AWS). All stored and transferred data is encrypted."
  Source: https://respond.io/security
- Retention (Privacy Policy): "We delete or restrict processing of data when it is no longer needed for its intended purpose"; "Server log files are deleted after 30 days"; CRM data reviewed "after two years at the end of each calendar year." (These retention windows describe respond.io's own website/CRM data, not necessarily customer conversation data — ambiguous as applied to message content.)
  Source: https://respond.io/privacy-policy

**5. Transparency to customers**
- Access-control framing (Security page): "Administrative sharing controls let you decide who on your organization has access to the platform. Add multiple users with different roles..."
  Source: https://respond.io/security
- The strongest transparency line acknowledging platform access: "Under no circumstances is sensitive data shared with anyone outside of respond.io and the client" — i.e., respond.io places itself inside the trust boundary rather than claiming zero-access.
  Source: https://respond.io/security

---

## TWILIO (as WhatsApp BSP / messaging processor)

**1. Controller vs. processor** *(DPA fetched directly; section labels lower-confidence)*
- "Twilio will process Customer Personal Data as a processor or sub-processor, rather than as a controller" (labeled Section 4.1).
- "Twilio is a processor or sub-processor (acting on behalf of Customer), except where Twilio processes Customer Personal Data as a controller" (labeled Section 2).
- "Customer may act as a controller or processor on behalf of its End Users" (labeled Section 2).
  Source: https://www.twilio.com/en-us/legal/data-protection-addendum

**2. Who can access message content**
- The DPA frames access via the instruction/least-privilege model rather than a blunt "Twilio can read messages" statement: "Twilio, as a processor or sub-processor, will process Customer Personal Data in accordance with Customer's instructions" (labeled Schedule 1, Sec 5).
  Source: https://www.twilio.com/en-us/legal/data-protection-addendum
- Security Overview (the clearest access acknowledgment): "Controlled and limited access of Customer Data strictly to authorized Twilio employees only..." — i.e., authorized Twilio employees CAN access Customer Data under controls.
  Source: https://www.twilio.com/en-us/legal/security-overview
- **BSP decryption point (the load-bearing technical fact for WhatsApp Cloud API).** Twilio's own blog confirms WhatsApp's E2E model terminates at a device/endpoint: "That end-to-end encryption requires all communication to flow through a 'device'... with each side using keys to encrypt and decrypt the payload," and "WhatsApp servers are purely there to help route the messages, remaining unable to decrypt or parse them in any way."
  Source: https://www.twilio.com/en-us/blog/building-the-twilio-api-for-whatsapp
- Meta's official Cloud API doc states the decryption happens at the Cloud API endpoint before reaching the business: "Once Cloud API receives the message, Cloud API decrypts the message and forwards it to the business," and "Cloud API manages the encryption/decryption keys on behalf of the business."
  Source: https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/data-privacy-and-security/
- **Net for the client's argument:** for WhatsApp Cloud API, E2E encryption ends at the Cloud API / business endpoint — the message is decrypted server-side and forwarded in plaintext to the business/BSP stack. So the BSP-layer processor (Twilio) and the business handle decrypted content; it is NOT end-to-end encrypted through to the BSP. This is confirmed by Meta's own doc and consistent with Twilio's blog. (Twilio's blog does not itself say "Twilio can read the content"; the decryption-at-endpoint fact comes from Meta's doc plus the architecture description.)

**3. Encryption**
- At rest (Security Overview): "Customer Data is encrypted at rest in AWS and GCP using the Advanced Encryption Standard."
- In transit (Security Overview): "Customer Data is encrypted when in transit between Customer's software application and the Services using TLS v1.2."
  Source: https://www.twilio.com/en-us/legal/security-overview

## Bottom line for the two platforms
- **Both are processors, not controllers** (customer/business = controller). Twilio states this explicitly in a public DPA; Respond.io only defines the terms in its Privacy Policy and gates the actual DPA behind an email request — so Respond.io's processor allocation is asserted but NOT publicly verifiable.
- **Both acknowledge platform/employee access to customer data** — neither claims a zero-knowledge / "we can't see your messages" architecture. Twilio: "authorized Twilio employees only." Respond.io: "outside of respond.io and the client" (respond.io is inside the boundary) + named internal staff categories.
- **Both encrypt in transit + at rest** (Twilio: AES at rest / TLS 1.2 in transit; Respond.io: 256-bit AES at rest / 256-bit SSL-TLS in transit).
- **WhatsApp E2E ends at the Cloud API/BSP endpoint** — Meta's own doc confirms Cloud API decrypts the message and forwards it to the business, and manages the keys on the business's behalf. So a WhatsApp BSP like Twilio processes decrypted content; the "end-to-end encryption" marketing does not extend through to the BSP layer.
